source_text: CAPUT TRICESIMUM TERTIUM, De harmonia rerum. HActenus de fato: sequitur harmonia, quae est magnus divini amoris influxus, praebens rebus modum, quo earum ordo consonat in bonum ac delectabilem finem. Quoniam nullus ordo propter se est, sed propter finem, finis autem optimum rerum: idcirco ordinis respectus ad finem nobis est harmonia, quae est multorum consonantia ad unum delectabile bonum, et e musicis hoc vocabulum sumpsimus, ubi in uno instrumento plures chordae, variae, crassae et graciles, variis tensae modis, arte praeeunte et cooperante, a musico pulsatae, suavem efficiunt melodiam ad animae delectationem. Quapropter harmonia videtur obiectum amoris, et quidem amoris activi influxus, sicuti fatum activae sapientiae, et sicuti amor est proles sapientiae, ita harmonia ordinis. Totius mundi harmoniam licet venari ex partibus. Videmus quidem omne agens agere propter finem et acquisito fine cessare actionem, et in bono finis agentem quiescere, sicut lapis tendit deorsum, quia apud consimile corpus servatur et cum est in suo consimili quiescit, quasi confessa causa motus; ignis vero sursum it et caelo adiunctus simul cum caelo circumfertur, quasi adeptus finem, qui in rei conservatione consistit.
english: CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE. On the harmony of things.

Thus far concerning fate: next comes harmony, which is the great influx of divine love, granting things a mode by which their order sounds together toward a good and delightful end. Because no order exists for its own sake but for an end, and the end is the best among things, therefore the respect of order to the end is for us harmony — the sounding-together of many things toward one delightful good. We have taken the word from music, where on one instrument many strings, varied, thick and thin, stretched in various ways, with art going before and cooperating, when struck by the musician produce a sweet melody for the delight of the soul.

Therefore harmony seems the object of love, and indeed of love as active influx, just as fate is of active wisdom; and as love is the offspring of wisdom, so harmony is the offspring of order. The harmony of the whole world may be hunted out from its parts. We see every agent act for an end, and when the end is gained the action ceases, and the agent rests in the good of the end — as a stone tends downward because it is preserved among like body and, once among its like, rests as if the cause of motion were confessed; but fire goes upward and, joined to heaven, is carried round with heaven as if it had attained the end that consists in the conservation of the thing.

source_text: At quia res omnes colligatae sunt loco et coexistentia et compactu, videmus alias aliarum esse fines, sicuti navigationis finis est mercatura, fabricationis navis finis est navigatio, dolationis lignorum est fabricatio, sectionis dolatio, et tamen hae artes inter se non communicant. Nam sector lignorum non secat ut dolentur, sed ut tali labore ipse victum quaerat. Qui vero dolat, non fabricationem intelligit, sed ea ab eo intelligitur qui eum conduxit, ipse vero mercedem intuetur. Qui navim fabricat ad navigationem, quatenus ab alio est non respicit, sed suum habet finem; nauta vero non respicit utrum merces bonae an inutiles sint, sed ut conficiat suum iter; de mercimonio enim curat mercator, de mercatura vero deque omnibus artibus caeteris simul curat respublica, quoniam in illarum communicatione eius consistit felicitas. Unde et Aristoteles bonum universi putat esse ordinem; sed nos id propter quod est ordo loquendo de bono intrinseco. Nam de extrinseco patet quod sit ipse Deus. Quoniam vero quaecunque necessario eveniunt ea ita ordinata sunt ut propter melius eveniant, prout necessitas ad potentiam, ordo ad sapientiam, harmonia melioris ad amorem referuntur. Eveniunt autem necessario omnia ex coactione quodammodo, eaque aut pura aut mixta amori, vel omnino libera. Libertas autem omnino in ipso uno Deo.
english: Yet because all things are bound together by place, coexistence, and compact, we see some to be ends of others — as the end of navigation is merchandise, of shipbuilding navigation, of hewing timber shipbuilding, of cutting hewing — and yet these arts do not communicate among themselves. For the cutter of timber does not cut so that it may be hewn, but that by such labor he may seek his living. He who hews does not understand the building; that is understood by the one who hired him, while he himself looks to his wage. He who builds a ship for navigation, insofar as he is hired by another, does not look to that further end but has his own; the sailor does not ask whether the wares are good or useless, but that he may finish his voyage; of the merchandise the merchant cares, but of trade and of all the other arts together the commonwealth cares, because its happiness consists in their communication.

Hence Aristotle too thinks the good of the universe is order; but we mean that for the sake of which order is, speaking of the intrinsic good. Of the extrinsic it is plain that it is God Himself. And because whatever happens necessarily is so ordered that it happens for the better — as necessity is referred to power, order to wisdom, and the harmony of the better to love — all things happen necessarily from a certain coercion, either pure or mixed with love, or else altogether free. Freedom altogether is in the one God alone.

source_text: Caeterae enim res aguntur ad proprium opus duobus eius sapientiae stimulis, voluptate scilicet et dolore, e quibus suboritur desiderium et metus, moeror et indignatio. Omnia autem quodammodo sentiunt proprium esse et amant; exteriora vero sentiunt et amant, in quantum sentiunt se ab illis immutari et affici. Unde si afficiuntur bene ad sui conservationem, delectantur; si male ad destructionem, oderunt et dolent. Deinde omnia videntur affici partim coacte, partim sponte, id est dolore et amore, semper praeeunte necessitate. Amare enim suum esse convenit unicuique ex eo quod non novit melius, ut canis amat se esse canem, et lignum tanquam lignum, quoniam proprium esse ut optimum noverunt, alia vero meliora esse ignorant; coguntur vero ignorare ex limitatione sui esse ac proinde coguntur et amare hoc unum, non autem amare simpliciter. Unde homines, qui aliam vitam et esse et sibi convenire post hanc ex religione vel ratione persuasum sibi habent, praesentem vitam spernunt, sese macerant et cupiunt dissolvi et esse cum Deo. Amor igitur vitae videtur quodammodo coactus, siquidem quicquid ignorantes melius facimus, ex parte coacte facimus. Unde et Seneca in Tragoedia: O quam mortalibus dulce malum additum, vitae dirus amor. Exteriora quoque cogimur amare, nempe cibum, vestem, labores et omnia quibus aliqualiter in nobis vel in aliis servamur. Cogimur quoque respectare res bonas in se tanquam nobis malas, ut ignem quia nos urit, et serpentem quia nos mordet, cicutam quia nos venenat: cum tamen in se et ad mundum et ad consimiles res omnes optimae sint et pulcherrimae.
english: For other things are driven to their proper work by two goads of His wisdom — namely pleasure and pain — from which arise desire and fear, grief and indignation. All things somehow sense their own being and love it; but they sense and love exterior things insofar as they sense themselves changed and affected by them. Hence if they are affected well toward their own conservation, they delight; if badly toward destruction, they hate and grieve.

Next, all things seem affected partly by force, partly spontaneously — that is, by pain and love — with necessity always going before. For to love ones own being belongs to each because it does not know a better: as a dog loves being a dog, and wood loves being wood, since they know their own being as best and are ignorant that other things are better. They are forced to that ignorance by the limitation of their being, and therefore forced also to love this one thing, not to love simply. Hence human beings who from religion or reason are persuaded that another life and being suit them after this one despise the present life, afflict themselves, and long to be dissolved and to be with God. Love of life therefore seems somehow forced, since whatever we do while ignorant of the better we do in part by force. Hence also Seneca in the Tragedy: O how sweet an evil added to mortals — the dread love of life.

We are forced also to love exterior things — food, clothing, labors, and all by which we are somehow preserved in ourselves or in others. We are forced also to regard things good in themselves as evil to us — fire because it burns us, the serpent because it bites, hemlock because it poisons — although in themselves and toward the world and toward like things they are all most excellent and most beautiful.

source_text: Sapientia vero aeterna utitur nostra ignorantia ad vitam nostram. Si enim singulae res scirent omnes alias res esse pulchras, utique nihil agerent contra invicem, nec propriam servarent vitam, omnia in chaos converterentur. Quapropter cum omnia sint bona et tuta, optimum est ad mundi ordinem ut videantur aliae res aliis malae et turpes, ne recidant in chaos. Et sane, qui ad authorem rerum se elevat et cum eo inspicit hanc quasi comoediam, in qua res omnes quibusdam personantur larvis, aliae apparent bonae et pulchrae, aliae malae et deformes, videt depositis larvis pulchre convenire. Affectiones et actiones a coactione et amore simul eduntur, et tunc vera est coactio, quando contra propensionem et amorem additum res aguntur. Sed ut serventur res in vita quam sortiuntur, dedit illis Deus dolorem et voluptatem. Gaudet enim homo esse in conservativis suae naturae, et dolet in destructivis. Et hoc est fatum, ut tanto tempore sint ut divino numini, quasi ad ludum et comoediam suam agendam, decretum est. Sed dicis: quare dum corrumpuntur res dolent, mortique quasi repugnant? Respondetur primo hoc fieri ne et caetera viventía ante suum tempus vellent mori. Secundo, ut dum moriuntur, repugnent causis afferentibus mortem ac modificent illas ad fati utilitates. Cum ergo omnes corruptiones et generationes rerum et actiones non sint propter ipsas res modo, quoniam ipsae dolore et voluptate aguntur ad fines aliorum, consequens est ut causa ordinatrix eliciat e talium ordine magnum divinumque bonum, quod vocamus HARMONIAM, quae fundatur in rerum esse et ordine, hoc est necessitate et fato. Omnia enim necessitate veniunt propter fatum et harmoniam. Ex his vero resultat harmonica bonitas, quae est finis rerum.
english: But eternal wisdom uses our ignorance for our life. For if each thing knew that all other things are beautiful, they would do nothing against one another, nor preserve their own life, and all would turn into chaos. Therefore, since all things are good and safe, it is best for the worlds order that some things appear to others evil and foul, lest they fall back into chaos. And truly, whoever lifts himself to the Author of things and with Him looks upon this as a comedy in which all things are masked by certain larvas — some appearing good and beautiful, others evil and deformed — sees that when the masks are laid aside they agree beautifully.

Affections and actions are brought forth from coercion and love together; and coercion is truly such when things are driven against their propensity and against the love added to them. But that things may be kept in the life they are allotted, God gave them pain and pleasure. For a human being rejoices to be among things that conserve his nature, and grieves among things that destroy it. And this is fate: that they exist for so long as has been decreed by the divine power, as for playing Its play and comedy.

But you say: why do things grieve when they are corrupted, and as it were resist death? It is answered, first, lest other living things also wish to die before their time; second, that while dying they may resist the causes bringing death and modify them for fates uses. Since therefore all corruptions and generations of things and actions are not for the sake of the things alone — because they themselves are driven by pain and pleasure toward others ends — it follows that the ordering cause draws from such order a great and divine good, which we call HARMONY, founded in the being and order of things, that is in necessity and fate. For all things come by necessity for the sake of fate and harmony. From these results the harmonic goodness that is the end of things.

source_text: II. Est autem cuiusque rei a DEO productae triplex finis: 1. conservationis sui, ad quam impellitur voluptate et dolore; 2. usus aliorum, ad quae impellitur metu et desiderio; 3. universi ordo et integritas, quae est propter Deum in harmonia et concursu causarum et necessitate prima. Sic planta facit fructus propter conservationem sui, ad quam timor mortis et amor vitae impellit, ex quo resultat secundus finis, qui est animalium nutricatus e fructibus eius, siquidem imperfecta entia sunt propter perfecta entia; animalium autem vita est ad mundi integritatem. Ergo finis plantae est mundi integritas. Sed quae immediatius attingunt ultimum finem, ea sunt caeteris nobiliora. Sunt autem rebus praeter proprium finem multi alii, qui mundo harmoniam pariunt, et quaecunque mala et excrementitia sunt, habent fines optimos. Sic humor cholericus unitur in felle, ne sanguinem inficiat, et quia vadit ad simile, vitalis est felli, ac deinde servit usibus magnis. Ex quibus manifestum est esse opificem rerum, qui ita disposuit et contemperavit res, ut dum pro se agunt singulae sint simul utiles aliis, et omnes toti, totum vero dedicatur et velificetur Dei gloriae. Harmonia igitur non consistit in eo duntaxat quod res quaelibet agat propter se, sed dum agit propter se, agat simul propter alia, et totum, et Deum. Et haec ordinis ratio est a sapientia prima. Sed pulchritudo oriens ab ordine est ab amore primo, et ipsa pulchritudo non ut signum quo rapimur ad boni notionem, sed ut influxus ab amore activo, est sedes harmoniae. Quapropter cum sapientissimus sit rerum opifex et omnia possit et sciat et naturae suae convenienter velit, omnia disponat et ordinet oportet. Nihil igitur est a casu respectu illius. Sic enim multa evenirent praeter necessitatem et praeter fatum et praeter harmoniam, et ipse subiectus esset fato et non fatum ipsi — id quod tam stultum et absurdum est, ac si artificem artis inventorem subiicias arti, non vero artem inventori. Ex quibus omnibus planum fit graviter errare Epicureos, Mahumedanos et alios, qui contra harmoniam omnia casu evenire opinantur, infringentes Dei potentiam, sapientiam et amorem, quo singulis sui praestituuntur fines, etiam noxiis animalibus, serpentibus, muscis ac similibus, imo et infirmitatibus. Neque ab hac harmonia excluduntur bella, pestis, fames et mors ipsa. Nam et haec utilia sunt mundo, sicut caloris et frigoris discordia, tum ad doctrinas inveniendas, tum ad regna mutanda, tum ad peccatorum punitionem, tum ad virtutis exercitium et variam demonstrationem.
english: II. Now of each thing produced by GOD there is a threefold end: first, conservation of itself, to which it is driven by pleasure and pain; second, the use of others, to which it is driven by fear and desire; third, the order and integrity of the universe, which is for God in the harmony and concurrence of causes and in the first necessity. So a plant makes fruit for its own conservation, to which fear of death and love of life drive it; from this results the second end, the nourishing of animals from its fruits, since imperfect beings exist for perfect ones; and the life of animals is for the integrity of the world. Therefore the end of the plant is the worlds integrity. But those that more immediately attain the last end are nobler than the rest.

Besides their proper end, things have many other ends that beget harmony for the world; and whatever is evil and excrementitious has most excellent ends. So choleric humor is gathered in the gall lest it infect the blood; and because it goes to its like, it is vital to the gall, and then serves great uses. From which it is plain there is a Craftsman of things who so disposed and tempered them that while each acts for itself it is at once useful to others, and all to the whole, and the whole is dedicated and set under sail for Gods glory. Harmony therefore does not consist only in each things acting for itself, but in this: that while it acts for itself it acts at once for others, for the whole, and for God.

And this reason of order is from the first wisdom. But the beauty rising from order is from the first love; and beauty itself, not as a sign by which we are carried to the notion of the good, but as an influx from active love, is the seat of harmony. Therefore, since the Craftsman of things is most wise and can and knows all things and wills according to His nature, He must dispose and order all things. Nothing therefore is by chance with respect to Him. Otherwise many things would happen beside necessity, beside fate, and beside harmony, and He Himself would be subject to fate and not fate to Him — which is as foolish and absurd as subjecting the inventor of an art to the art rather than the art to the inventor.

From all of which it becomes plain that the Epicureans, Muhammadans, and others gravely err who against harmony think all things happen by chance, breaking Gods power, wisdom, and love, by which ends are appointed even to harmful animals, serpents, flies and the like, and even to infirmities. Nor are wars, plague, famine, and death itself excluded from this harmony. For these too are useful to the world, as the discord of heat and cold — for inventing doctrines, for changing kingdoms, for punishing sins, and for the exercise and varied demonstration of virtue.
